featured_reviews.review_text:
The care given is really good.
My mother was admitted here. They give personalized attention and good care.
The doctors are well experienced, attentive and explain you everything properly.
The staff is very helpful when it comes to solving any problem.
You are not allowed to get your food. So, if you are a patient's relative, as a local guide I would suggest don't fall for canteen food. The canteen food mostly offers biscuits and stuff like misal pav vada. 1-2 protein bars which are processed.

There is a seperate menu from which you can order food which offers options like Khichadi and dahi which are decent.
Because, when your relatives is admitted in the hospital neglecting your own health and falling for sugary oily food may not be a good option.

I would suggest they have seperate menu, which you will need to call a number and ask for, there you get better options than the processed food.

There is personalised dietician assigned to each patient. She mostly gives balanced options for the patients. I had seen Marie Biscuit in my mom's diet. I personally don't want my mom to eat biscuits with palm oil in it. So, she switched the snack.
So, if you have special preferences. You can always communicate.

One more suggestion to the hospital.
If you have a room patient's relative mostly gets assigned bed.
But if the patient is in the ICU there is no assigned bed for the patient's relative. Which is mostly offered in some other hospitals. So, that could be added.

featured_reviews.review_text:
My sister recently delivered her baby here, and our overall experience was average.

Throughout the pregnancy, we were asked to undergo multiple scans and make several visits. While we understand the importance of regular monitoring, it did feel like some of them may not have been necessary.

The room provided was quite compact and felt a bit suffocating. The beds were small and not very comfortable. My mother stayed with my sister, and the accompanying bed was also quite uncomfortable for her. Additionally, the room did not appear to be maintained as neatly as expected.

One major concern was the mosquito issue, especially during the evening. There were quite a lot of mosquitoes around the building and even inside the room. Unfortunately, the newborn was also bitten by mosquitoes, and my sister was unable to get proper rest post-delivery. This was quite disappointing, as undisturbed sleep and a hygienic environment are basic necessities for both mother and baby in a hospital setting.

Considering the charges, we expected better cleanliness, room comfort, and overall maintenance. We also found that the staff was not helpful regarding government benefits available for a newborn girl child, which added to our disappointment.

That said, I would like to appreciate the post-delivery consultation sessions covering various aspects of care. They were genuinely helpful and well-conducted. Kudos to the team for that, and I hope this continues.

Overall, there is definite scope for improvement in cleanliness, room setup, staff guidance, and especially resolving the mosquito issue so that the experience better matches the cost and expectations.

featured_reviews.name: Lavina Dsouza
featured_reviews.review_text:
This was my first visit to Arya Hospital, and no doubt Dr. Vidya Patil was very polite and approachable however the overall experience could be significantly improved through better patient privacy, staff training, clear communication, and time management.

Firstly I got at appointment for 12:00 pm only to be attended at 1.40 pm which is a wait time approximately 1.5 hours for a consultation that lasted barely 15 minutes.
Personal and sensitive medical questions were asked in front of other patients, compromising ones privacy.
Staff appeared inadequately trained, as my blood pressure was initially recorded incorrectly. Later during consultation only after I pointed it out was the diagnosis reconsidered and the incorrect BP reading influenced the whole check up. Which was not appropriate.
Additional sonography tests were conducted on the spot, but the purpose, findings, and implications were not explained clearly. I had to repeatedly ask probing questions to understand symptoms, and recommended precautions. But the response was not precise or satisfactory. Also it's a personal decision, such as choosing not to have children, which should be approached with sensitivity and professionalism. Such choices should not be casually linked to a patient's medical concerns without clear medical reasoning and discussion.

While healthcare professionals may see hundreds of patients, for each patient that consultation is a significant moment to seek clarity, understanding, and reassurance about their health.
